additions.decisiveConstraint: The material-exception quality floor is a hard business requirement, so efficiency cannot justify a path that fails it.
additions.expectedDecision: Use the stronger model for the exception workload or route it to a validated stronger or human path, and retain the efficient model only where its measured quality clears the applicable floor.
additions.rationale: Value alignment can favor higher capability when a consequence-bearing quality floor is explicit and the route remains operationally feasible.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Use the efficient model for all appeals because its lower cost maximizes productivity.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The efficient path misses the material-exception floor and shifts error cost into appeals without meeting the business outcome.
additions.counterfactual: If the efficient model cleared 97% on the same held-out slice, use it as the default and test a stronger route only for measured residual failures.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends evaluating model capabilities, speed, cost, and effort against the actual use case rather than optimizing one dimension alone.
additions.auditFinding: Adds the quality-first reversal of the current efficient default, with a quantified floor and feasible cost/latency boundary.
additions.contrastBeforeDecision: The existing item has a measured efficient candidate whose quality is sufficient for the stated routine workload.
additions.contrastAfterDecision: This item makes material-exception recall a hard floor that the efficient model misses, so the stronger route is required.

additions.scenario: A claims triage service handles 50,000 cases per month: 40,000 routine and 10,000 high-impact cases. On the same held-out routine and high-impact classes, the efficient model scores 97% and 91%, costs $0.02 per case, and runs at 1.2 seconds p95; the stronger model scores 98% and 96%, costs $0.15, and runs at 2.3 seconds p95.
additions.evidence: The high-impact quality floor is 95%, the service p95 limit is 2.5 seconds, and the monthly model budget is $2,500. All-efficient costs $1,000 but fails the high-impact floor; all-stronger costs $7,500; routing the 10,000 high-impact cases to the stronger model and routine cases to the efficient model costs $2,300. A classifier identifies high-impact cases with 94% precision, and reviewers handle residual uncertainty.
additions.decisiveConstraint: Both models were measured on the same classes, so the decision must satisfy the 95% high-impact floor, 2.5-second p95 limit, and $2,500 monthly budget together.
additions.expectedDecision: Use the efficient model for routine cases and the stronger model for identified high-impact cases, confirm the routed mix stays under the 2.5-second end-to-end p95 and $2,500 budget, and send classifier-uncertain high-impact cases to the bounded reviewer queue.
additions.rationale: The worked monthly costs and same-class outcomes make segmented routing the only stated design that meets the high-impact floor without exceeding budget or latency.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Use the stronger model for every case because its acceptance rate is higher, or the efficient model for every case because its monthly price is lower.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: All-stronger exceeds the $2,500 budget by $5,000, while all-efficient misses the 95% high-impact floor; the stronger route is feasible at 2.3 seconds only for the high-impact slice.
additions.counterfactual: If the stronger route measured above 2.5 seconds end to end under the routed load, reject that route for the hard-deadline slice and use a reviewed asynchronous or narrower escalation path; if its cost fell below the global budget, broaden only after the same class gates pass.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends evaluating model capabilities, speed, cost, and effort against the actual use case rather than optimizing one dimension alone.
additions.auditFinding: Adds a worked same-class comparison with hard quality, p95, classifier, and monthly cost thresholds, replacing the earlier non-comparable routine-versus-complex figures.
additions.integrationConstraint: D3.3 owns the 2.5-second end-to-end tail and queue behavior for the routed mix; if stronger-model load breaks p95, the expected decision changes from high-impact routing to a smaller escalation or reviewer path even though the same-class quality floor remains.

objectiveLabel: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs

existing.scenario: A retailer classifies 50,000 short product questions per hour under low-latency and low-cost targets with a held-out quality gate.
existing.evidence: The workload is high-volume and relatively straightforward; real questions are available for testing.
existing.decisiveConstraint: Start with the least costly and fastest candidate that meets measured task quality, then upgrade only for demonstrated gaps.
existing.expectedDecision: Test an efficient model on representative questions and escalate or upgrade only if the quality slice requires it.
existing.rationale: Model choice follows the workload's capability, speed, and cost evidence rather than public rank or maximum capability.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Keep the strongest model permanently because capability dominates every criterion.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: It ignores unit-cost and latency constraints and assumes extra capability is needed without test evidence.
existing.counterfactual: If the held-out set showed a material quality gap on common cases, the stronger model or a measured route would become necessary.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends starting with a faster, cost-effective model for many workloads, testing thoroughly, and upgrading only when performance gaps require it.
existing.auditFinding: The model decision is sound, but option b is strictly longest; rewrite all options to comparable evaluation detail and keep business SLA ownership with D1.6.

existing.scenario: A compliance classifier meets average accuracy but misses rare jurisdictional exceptions because the small model was chosen only for price.
existing.evidence: The failing slice is identifiable and a real exception benchmark can be built.
existing.decisiveConstraint: Compare candidate model capability, edge-case quality, latency, and cost on actual prompts before changing production.
existing.expectedDecision: Run slice-based benchmarks and then choose a model change, route, or human path only if evidence shows a capability gap.
existing.rationale: Average accuracy hides the decision-relevant failures; measured slices distinguish model capability from prompt or routing fixes.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Replace the model with the most expensive tier immediately.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Higher price does not prove the candidate fixes the exception slice or fits service constraints.
existing.counterfactual: If the expensive candidate failed the same exceptions, the correct response would be a better prompt, retrieval, or human route rather than an upgrade.
existing.sourceSection: Decide whether to upgrade or change models
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends benchmark tests using actual prompts and data, then comparing accuracy, quality, edge cases, and cost.
existing.auditFinding: The slice-based diagnosis is correct, but option c is strictly longest; rebalance options and preserve a credible alternative involving prompt or routing repair.

existing.scenario: A scientific assistant performs complex multi-hour investigations where nuanced reasoning matters more than interactive price.
existing.evidence: The team can evaluate the real workflow and optimize later; no fixed low-latency SLA is stated.
existing.decisiveConstraint: Establish a capability-first quality floor before reducing model effort or tier.
existing.expectedDecision: Start with the strongest suitable capability, evaluate representative research, then optimize where quality remains acceptable.
existing.rationale: A weak baseline would make it impossible to know whether later efficiency changes preserve the required research quality.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Start with the cheapest model because all requests are text.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Input modality and price do not establish reasoning quality, edge-case coverage, or research usefulness.
existing.counterfactual: If the workload were routine high-volume classification with a strict p95 and unit-cost target, efficiency-first testing would be appropriate.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends a capability-first starting point for complex reasoning and accuracy-sensitive work, followed by evaluation and efficiency optimization.
existing.auditFinding: The capability-first boundary is sound, but option a is strictly longest; rewrite alternatives with comparable quality and optimization evidence.

existing.scenario: A support platform has routine delivery questions and difficult account-recovery cases with separate quality, latency, and cost benchmarks.
existing.evidence: Workload segments differ in capability and risk; route outcomes are measurable.
existing.decisiveConstraint: Use an efficient path for routine work and stronger capability or human review for measured difficult cases.
existing.expectedDecision: Route routine cases to a validated efficient model and difficult or high-risk cases to a stronger model or human path.
existing.rationale: Measured routing preserves the quality floor while avoiding universal use of the most expensive model.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Use the strongest model for every request or route by message length alone.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Universal strength wastes cost and latency; length is an unreliable proxy for sensitive reasoning difficulty.
existing.counterfactual: If all requests had the same benchmark and no route could be measured reliably, one validated model would be safer than an opaque router.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic describes multi-model strategies that use a lower-cost executor for most work and escalate difficult decisions to a stronger advisor or model.
existing.auditFinding: Controller inspected every canonical option: preserve the useful scenario and decision, but replace implausible distractors that advertise unsafe, unmeasured, untyped, arbitrary, or explicitly unverified behavior; provide professional competing actions that lose on the stated constraint and align per-option feedback.

additions.scenario: An invoice deployment currently sends external OCR text to Claude, but photographs of damaged forms contain handwritten totals that OCR omits; the team can benchmark direct image input to the same target model if image support is enabled.
additions.evidence: Paired representative cases compare the current OCR text request with a direct-image request; the direct-image path preserves handwritten totals in evaluation but has measured latency and cost.
additions.decisiveConstraint: Choose an input path only after verifying the target model accepts image content and meets the handwritten-field accuracy floor; text-path scores alone cannot establish that capability.
additions.expectedDecision: Run a paired capability benchmark for OCR text and direct-image requests to the target Claude model, then choose direct image when its measured accuracy gain justifies latency and cost; otherwise retain OCR with a manual or rejected-field path.
additions.rationale: The decision tests an actual supported input modality on the production failure slice without inventing a separate candidate-model catalog.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Assume OCR text is sufficient because the invoice schema is structured and choose the lowest measured text-processing cost.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The current OCR path has already removed handwritten evidence, so a strong text result cannot recover the missing totals.
additions.counterfactual: If OCR preserved every required field at the same accuracy floor and direct-image input added cost without benefit, the OCR text path would remain justified.
additions.sourceClaim: Claude accepts image content blocks for visual analysis. Choosing direct images over an OCR-only pipeline here depends on the stated paired workload measurements, not a guaranteed accuracy advantage.
additions.auditFinding: Uncovered model decision: verify and benchmark direct image input versus the current OCR path on the actual handwritten-field slice; this avoids assuming unverified text-only candidates.

additions.scenario: A code assistant must produce repository patches that pass a typed output contract; candidate models have similar code-review scores but differ sharply in valid patch rate.
additions.evidence: The service can replay representative tasks and measure parseable patches, test pass rate, latency, and cost by model.
additions.decisiveConstraint: The production model must satisfy the output contract and task quality, not only a general capability benchmark.
additions.expectedDecision: Select the candidate whose measured valid-patch and test-pass floors hold on the target repositories, then compare cost and latency before rollout.
additions.rationale: Output-contract reliability is a task capability that can change the model decision even when broad quality scores look equivalent.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Choose by public coding benchmark rank and treat malformed patches as an application parsing problem.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: A benchmark rank does not establish the repository's output contract, and repeated parse failures remain a model-path cost and quality problem.
additions.counterfactual: If every candidate produced the same valid-patch floor, latency and cost could decide the model without this capability distinction.
additions.sourceSection: Decide whether to upgrade or change models
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends testing with actual prompts and data and weighing performance and cost tradeoffs against use-case benchmarks.
additions.auditFinding: Uncovered model decision: treat valid output-contract rate as a capability criterion alongside task quality; distinct from raw benchmark and latency-only choices.

additions.scenario: A tax-law assistant drafts positions for rare jurisdictional exceptions. The efficient model is 1.0 second p95 and $0.03 per case but reaches 88% on the exception rubric; the stronger model is 2.8 seconds and $0.12 but reaches 97%. The service allows 4 seconds and the legal quality floor is 95%.
additions.evidence: The exception slice is consequence-bearing, has a held-out evaluation set, and is a small fraction of traffic; a reviewer handles unresolved cases.
additions.decisiveConstraint: Capability and quality are the gating criteria for this workload, so the efficient-first default must reverse when it fails the hard exception floor.
additions.expectedDecision: Start with the stronger suitable model for the exception workflow, validate it on representative cases, then test a lower-cost route only where quality remains above 95%.
additions.rationale: The stronger model is feasible within the stated latency and satisfies the consequence-bearing floor that the efficient model misses.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Start with the efficient model for all cases and upgrade only after broad production complaints appear.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: Waiting for complaints ignores the held-out evidence and exposes legal decisions to a known quality failure.
additions.counterfactual: If the efficient model reached 95% on the exception slice at 1.0 second, retain it and optimize cost before considering a stronger model.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends a capability-first starting point for complex reasoning and accuracy-sensitive work, followed by evaluation and efficiency optimization.
additions.auditFinding: True reversal of the existing efficiency-first model choice under a measured complex, accuracy-sensitive exception workload.
additions.contrastBeforeDecision: The existing paired item has high-volume short questions with a quality gate and no stated capability floor that the efficient model cannot meet.
additions.contrastAfterDecision: This item makes exception quality a hard 95% floor and keeps the stronger route inside the latency budget.

additions.scenario: A support classifier receives 40 requests per second. On the same held-out routine and high-risk classes, Model A scores 97% and 93% with 0.7 seconds p95, while Model B scores 98% and 99% with 1.4 seconds p95. A risk detector identifies high-risk traffic with 92% precision and 97% recall.
additions.evidence: The service p95 limit is 1.2 seconds, the high-risk quality floor is 98%, and the budget permits Model B for at most 20% of requests. An end-to-end labeled replay including detector false negatives measures 98.8% high-risk accuracy for the routed system. Load tests measure 1.1 seconds p95 and Model B use on 18% of requests; Model B for all traffic reaches 1.9 seconds p95. Unrecognized false negatives follow the ordinary route and are included in the measured quality result.
additions.decisiveConstraint: The measured routed system, including false negatives, clears the high-risk quality floor, latency limit, and Model B allocation. Detector precision or model-only accuracy alone would not establish this.
additions.expectedDecision: Use Model A for routine requests and Model B for the detected high-risk slice, retain the separately flagged uncertainty review path, and monitor end-to-end high-risk accuracy including detector misses, routing volume, and 1.2-second p95 under production concurrency.
additions.rationale: Both models are compared on the same classes and the routed outcome includes the detector-miss path, so the mixed strategy is selected from measured end-to-end behavior rather than incomparable per-class claims.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Use Model B globally for its higher accuracy or Model A globally for its lower latency.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The global stronger route breaches p95 and budget, while the global efficient route fails the high-risk floor; the measured mixed route includes unrecognized false negatives in its end-to-end quality result and clears the stated floor.
additions.counterfactual: If end-to-end high-risk accuracy including detector misses fell below 98%, or mixed-route p95 exceeded 1.2 seconds, hold the affected rollout and redesign the route instead of inferring readiness from model-only scores.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic describes multi-model strategies that use a lower-cost executor for most work and escalate difficult decisions to a stronger advisor or model.
additions.auditFinding: Adds an integrated model selection case with both-model same-class scores and measured routed outcomes, including the detector-miss path and end-to-end tail.
additions.integrationConstraint: D3.3 requires queue-aware end-to-end p95 and routed-slice quality at 40 requests per second, including unrecognized detector misses; failure of either measured floor changes the decision from rollout to a hold and routing redesign.

objectiveLabel: Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails

existing.scenario: A support assistant summarizes a ticket, retrieves policy, drafts a reply, and must abstain when policy evidence is missing.
existing.evidence: A specialist sends the reply; policy grounding and explicit escalation are required.
existing.decisiveConstraint: The prompt must establish role, delimited context, sequence, output schema, and abstention behavior.
existing.expectedDecision: Use structured instructions and tagged policy/ticket sections with a machine-checkable handoff state.
existing.rationale: Explicit prompt boundaries reduce instruction ambiguity and make missing evidence observable.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Tell Claude to be helpful and rely on general knowledge for difficult tickets.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: General knowledge can conflict with policy and offers no deterministic escalation condition.
existing.counterfactual: If policy were not authoritative and the assistant only generated informal suggestions, the strict abstention and policy-delimited contract could be relaxed.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends clear, explicit instructions and descriptive XML tags to separate instructions, context, examples, and inputs.
existing.auditFinding: The prompt design is valid, but option d is strictly longest by a wide margin; rewrite choices with comparable contract detail and preserve a credible structured alternative.

existing.scenario: A procurement prompt sometimes treats a supplier's instruction to ignore policy as governing system instruction.
existing.evidence: Supplier text is untrusted input; procurement policy remains authoritative.
existing.decisiveConstraint: The prompt must make authority and untrusted content structurally distinct.
existing.expectedDecision: Use descriptive sections for instructions, policy, and supplier message, and state precedence explicitly.
existing.rationale: Tags and authority instructions target the parsing failure directly without changing model size.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Repeat the supplier message or move policy below it and ask Claude to reconcile implicitly.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Repetition can amplify injection and implicit reconciliation preserves the authority ambiguity.
existing.counterfactual: If supplier text were independently sanitized and stored outside the prompt, the prompt still needs a data contract but injection separation would be a lower-risk diagnosis.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic says XML tags help Claude parse complex prompts unambiguously when instructions, context, examples, and variables are mixed.
existing.auditFinding: The injection diagnosis is sound, but option b is strictly longest; rewrite options with comparable authority-boundary specificity.

existing.scenario: A credit assistant proposes amounts through a tool whose service currently accepts values above the account limit without approval.
existing.evidence: Credit issuance changes external state; the limit must hold even when model output is wrong.
existing.decisiveConstraint: Non-negotiable authorization and limits must execute at the service boundary, with approval for high-impact actions.
existing.expectedDecision: Enforce limits and authorization server-side, require confirmation or human approval for high-impact credits, and use the prompt as guidance.
existing.rationale: Prompt instructions are not a substitute for deterministic enforcement of an external side effect.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Repeat the limit sentence and trust Claude's confidence score.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Prompt repetition and model confidence do not enforce a limit against malformed or manipulated tool arguments.
existing.counterfactual: If the tool were read-only and returned no external mutation, prompt guidance could be sufficient for the interaction boundary, though output validation would remain useful.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic's tool guide states that the application writes the schema and executes custom tool calls, so the application remains the enforcement boundary.
existing.auditFinding: The server-side guardrail is correct, but option c is strictly longest; rewrite choices with comparable enforcement detail and avoid a length cue.

existing.scenario: A logistics assistant shares a workflow across regions; regional values vary and missing data must be visible rather than guessed.
existing.evidence: The common role and output contract are stable; validated regional variables are available.
existing.decisiveConstraint: Separate reusable governing instructions from changing data and represent missing fields explicitly.
existing.expectedDecision: Use a reusable system template with validated variables and a structured missing-data state that routes clarification.
existing.rationale: Stable prompt behavior can be reused without allowing dynamic data to rewrite authority or invent absent facts.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Rewrite the system prompt per request or ask for a fluent estimate when a field is absent.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Per-request rewrites drift and invented values make complete-looking output unreliable.
existing.counterfactual: If regions had genuinely different workflows and policies, separate versioned templates would be warranted instead of one shared contract.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends explicit instructions, desired output formats, and constraints so Claude does not have to infer the team's workflow.
existing.auditFinding: Controller inspected every canonical option: preserve the useful scenario and decision, but replace implausible distractors that advertise unsafe, unmeasured, untyped, arbitrary, or explicitly unverified behavior; provide professional competing actions that lose on the stated constraint and align per-option feedback.

additions.scenario: A pricing assistant receives two approved templates: the regional template says round to whole units, while the finance template says preserve cents; both are trusted and the overlap is producing inconsistent answers.
additions.evidence: The templates have owners and versions, but no precedence or condition states which rule controls an overlapping request.
additions.decisiveConstraint: The system prompt must make authority and conditional precedence explicit before generation; merely displaying both trusted templates leaves a deterministic conflict unresolved.
additions.expectedDecision: Tag each template, define the canonical precedence and the condition for regional versus finance rounding in the system prompt, and route any unmatched conflict to an explicit clarification state.
additions.rationale: This is a prompt-contract decision for contradictory trusted instructions, distinct from defending against untrusted supplier text or validating a numeric field after generation.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Place both templates in the prompt and ask Claude to reconcile the conflict from wording and recency.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: Implicit reconciliation can vary by phrasing and offers no auditable rule for the same overlapping request.
additions.counterfactual: If the templates covered disjoint fields with no possible overlap, separate tagged sections would be sufficient without a precedence rule.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic advises being clear and direct about instructions, desired output, and constraints; encoding canonical precedence and conditional rules here is the scenario's prompt-contract application.
additions.auditFinding: Uncovered prompt decision: encode canonical precedence and conditional rules for conflicting trusted templates; this is distinct from generic source delimiting and post-generation validation.

additions.scenario: A customer email template changed one variable from {due_date} to {payment_due_date}; after deployment, outputs occasionally contain the old literal placeholder even though the surrounding instructions are unchanged.
additions.evidence: The template catalog is versioned, render tests can run against representative records, and the failure begins at the single variable change.
additions.decisiveConstraint: A variable or template change must be controlled as a versioned prompt contract with a render regression check, rather than hidden by a generic caution instruction.
additions.expectedDecision: Publish a new version of the canonical template, update the variable schema and examples together, run representative render and placeholder checks, and roll back or reject the version on failure.
additions.rationale: The repair targets a localized prompt-template contract change and makes its effect measurable without adding unrelated guardrails.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Normalize unresolved variable names in model output with a postprocessor, retain the deployed template, and monitor placeholder frequency.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The postprocessor cannot reliably recover the missing value or prove which field the template intended; repairing and testing the render contract addresses the version-specific defect before generation.
additions.counterfactual: If the variable name were unchanged and the issue came from untrusted user text, authority-boundary design would be the relevant prompt repair instead.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends establishing clear success criteria and empirical tests before improving a prompt; versioning and render checks here are scenario-authored controls for the changed template contract.
additions.auditFinding: Uncovered prompt decision: version and test a single template-variable change against a controlled render contract; this is distinct from adding more safety instructions.

additions.scenario: A claims assistant returns {decision: approve, limit: 5000} in the required JSON schema and cites policy revision P17. The retrieved P17 passage requires manager approval but states no 5,000 limit; that amount appears only in a stale P12 chunk. The response is about to be sent to an analyst.
additions.evidence: The schema validator passes and P17 is on the approved source list. A claim-to-span check can compare each material field with the current retrieved passage, and a specialist can review an escalation.
additions.decisiveConstraint: Structural validity and citation presence do not establish that a material claim is supported by the cited current evidence.
additions.expectedDecision: After parsing, check each material field against its current evidence span; mark the unsupported limit unknown and abstain or escalate rather than send the approval. Keep authorization checks as a separate gate.
additions.rationale: This isolates factual grounding from the JSON contract and from permission to invoke an external action. An allowlisted citation can still fail to entail the value returned.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Accept any schema-valid object with an allowlisted citation and rely on the analyst to correct occasional unsupported values.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: A valid shape and source ID can hide a stale or invented value, and post-send correction does not prevent an unsupported approval from being acted on.
additions.counterfactual: If every output field were computed from typed fields in a validated policy record, deterministic field mapping could establish support without a separate model entailment check.
additions.sourceSection: Long context prompting — Ground responses in quotes
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends structuring long document context and asking Claude to ground responses in relevant document passages; the field-to-span gate and escalation are scenario controls.
additions.auditFinding: Uncovered decision: distinguish a schema-valid, cited response from a factually supported response and abstain on an unsupported material field.

additions.scenario: A claims assistant returns {decision: approve, limit: 5000} in the required JSON schema and cites policy revision P17. The current P17 passage explicitly supports a 5,000 limit, records the required manager approval, and the account scope is valid; a stale P12 passage is also present but is not the governing revision.
additions.evidence: Field-level checks can bind decision and limit to the P17 evidence span, bind approval to record A88, verify the current account scope, and preserve the policy revision in the analyst handoff.
additions.decisiveConstraint: The current governing evidence and approval record support every material field, so the assistant should produce a grounded ready-for-analyst result while retaining separate execution authorization.
additions.expectedDecision: Parse the schema, verify the decision and limit against the current P17 span and approval A88, include those references in the analyst handoff, mark the result grounded and ready for analyst review, and leave any final credit execution behind the service authorization gate.
additions.rationale: The evidence state changes from unsupported stale text to complete current support; grounding requires delivery with references, not abstention simply because an older conflicting passage exists.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Abstain because another retrieved passage says the amount is unsupported, and send no recommendation even though P17 is current and approval A88 is valid.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The older P12 passage is not the governing revision, while current P17 and A88 support the result; abstention would discard valid evidence without resolving the actual authority order.
additions.counterfactual: If P17 omitted the limit or A88 were missing or the account scope invalid, return to the sibling decision: mark the unsupported field unknown and abstain or escalate.
additions.sourceSection: Long context prompting — Ground responses in quotes
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends structuring long document context and asking Claude to ground responses in relevant document passages; the field-to-span gate and escalation are scenario controls.
additions.auditFinding: True reversal of the sibling stale-evidence case: current P17, valid approval, and valid scope support a grounded analyst handoff while execution remains separately authorized.
additions.contrastBeforeDecision: The existing paired item has a P17 passage without the claimed limit and a stale P12 passage that supplies it, so the limit is unsupported and must be unknown/abstained.
additions.contrastAfterDecision: This item has current P17 evidence for 5,000, approval A88, and valid account scope, so the grounded result can be delivered to the analyst.

additions.scenario: Prompt version 7 adds a conditional refusal rule and a risk_reason field to a claims assistant. On a 10,000-case replay, JSON validity falls from 99.6% to 96.8%, correct refusals rise from 93% to 97%, p95 is unchanged, and the production floor is 99% valid output.
additions.evidence: Every invalid record is traceable to prompt version and field-level parser error, while the refusal improvement matters for high-risk claims. The service can canary and roll back a template version.
additions.decisiveConstraint: The safer refusal behavior is valuable, but the prompt contract cannot ship below the output validity floor; revise the contract and guardrail together with observable outcomes.
additions.expectedDecision: Keep the refusal requirement, revise the schema/template examples so risk_reason is emitted only under the documented condition, replay the cases, and canary only a version that clears 99% validity while retaining the refusal gain.
additions.rationale: The conflicting safety and contract metrics require a versioned prompt decision plus field-level observability rather than choosing one aggregate metric.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Ship version 7 because correct refusals improved, then let downstream parsers handle the 3.2% invalid records.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: Invalid records breach the production contract and make downstream handling unsafe; unchanged latency does not make malformed decisions acceptable.
additions.counterfactual: If revised version 8 reaches 99.2% validity with at least 96% correct refusals, canary it; if not, keep version 6 and escalate the unresolved safety requirement.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends establishing clear success criteria and empirical tests before improving a prompt; versioning and render checks here are scenario-authored controls for the changed template contract.
additions.auditFinding: Adds an integrated prompt and telemetry decision with conflicting measured outcomes, distinct from the existing variable-name regression.
additions.integrationConstraint: D3.4 requires prompt-version, field-error, refusal, and deployment-slice traces to separate a contract regression from a safety gain; without those joins, the expected decision is hold or roll back rather than tune blindly.

objectiveLabel: Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)

existing.scenario: An invoice extractor has a documented JSON schema and familiar fields but no representative labeled examples yet.
existing.evidence: The task can be specified directly; representative invoices can be evaluated after prompting.
existing.decisiveConstraint: Choose a baseline technique that does not invent demonstrations and keeps the output contract explicit.
existing.expectedDecision: Start with a clear zero-shot prompt and evaluate it before adding examples or reasoning guidance.
existing.rationale: Zero-shot gives a clean baseline when the schema and field definitions are known but examples are unavailable.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Add fabricated examples or ask for an essay before extraction.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Fabricated examples can teach accidental patterns, while prose adds tokens without clarifying the requested fields.
existing.counterfactual: If real diverse labeled invoices existed and failures clustered around layouts, relevant few-shot examples could be the next experiment.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic advises being specific about desired output format and constraints, which supports a measurable zero-shot baseline.
existing.auditFinding: The technique choice is sound, but option a is strictly longest; rebalance alternatives to comparable schema and evaluation detail.

existing.scenario: A moderation classifier handles ordinary messages but reverses decisions on sarcasm, quoted abuse, and reclaimed terms.
existing.evidence: The difficult cases are labeled and can be represented with varied examples.
existing.decisiveConstraint: The prompt must teach the ambiguous decision boundary without overfitting one wording pattern.
existing.expectedDecision: Add a small diverse, relevant few-shot set in explicit example tags and evaluate edge and ordinary slices.
existing.rationale: Contrasting examples show how the policy applies where an abstract rule is underspecified.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Repeat one difficult example or remove classification criteria.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Repetition overfits wording and removing criteria removes the governing distinction.
existing.counterfactual: If no representative labeled examples existed, use an explicit zero-shot rubric first and collect labels before few-shot tuning.

additions.scenario: A customer-support prompt prepends a fresh customer transcript, cart, exchange rate, and request-specific entitlement on every turn. additions.decisiveConstraint: There is no worthwhile eligible stable prefix to cache in this prompt shape, so the design must preserve current authorization state and avoid padding or moving volatile data into a purported cache prefix.
additions.expectedDecision: Keep the safety header and current user state in their explicit roles, do not pad the prompt or claim cache reuse, and accept the absence of an eligible cache prefix until a genuinely stable contract or policy block exists.
additions.rationale: Prompt reuse depends on exact stable bytes and provider eligibility; forcing a cache breakpoint around volatile state creates misses and token cost rather than safe reuse.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Repeat static phrases or place the volatile customer state before a breakpoint to reach the cache threshold and maximize prompt reuse.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: Repeated padding does not make the changing transcript, cart, rate, or entitlement stable; exact-prefix comparison will miss and the extra tokens increase cost.
additions.counterfactual: If a versioned role and policy block became stable and long enough for provider eligibility, place that exact block before the breakpoint and keep per-request state after it.
additions.sourceClaim: Prompt caching matches the cumulative prefix at a breakpoint; changed content before that breakpoint produces a different prefix.
additions.auditFinding: True contrast of cache eligibility: the existing item has a stable versioned tenant policy prefix, while this prompt has only a 100-token stable header below the provider minimum and must not be padded.
additions.contrastBeforeDecision: The existing paired item has stable safety instructions and a versioned tenant policy large enough to place before a cache breakpoint.
additions.contrastAfterDecision: This item has an all-changing long prefix and only a 100-token stable header below eligibility, so no cache prefix should be forced.

additions.scenario: A policy release changes the current support policy from P41 to P42. Cache-hit rate remains 92%, but 0.6% of responses cite P41 after rollout; a trace of the actually assembled request shows the application still fetched and placed P41 before the cache breakpoint.
additions.evidence: Provider prompt caching reuses exact matching prefix bytes, so a request assembled with P42 would not match the old P41 prefix. The application can trace policy fetch, assembled prefix revision, cache hit/miss, and outcome, and canary the corrected fetch path.
additions.decisiveConstraint: The stale response is an application policy-fetch/assembly defect; repair current-policy selection before the cache call and use version/outcome joins to prove the fix.
additions.expectedDecision: Fix the policy fetch and assembly path to place current P42 bytes before the breakpoint, canary responses with the actual assembled revision and outcome, and retain provider cache behavior; do not claim the unchanged provider cache served changed bytes.
additions.rationale: Exact-prefix semantics turn the observed P41 assembly into the decisive evidence: current P42 bytes would naturally miss the P41 prefix, so application freshness is the repair boundary.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Invalidate the provider cache or treat 92% hits as proof that the provider is reusing stale content, without inspecting the assembled request.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The provider compares exact prefix bytes; the trace already shows the application supplied P41, so provider invalidation would not repair the stale fetch path and would hide the root cause.
additions.counterfactual: If the assembled request showed P42 but responses still cited P41, inspect downstream retrieval or response attribution; if P42 bytes were never assembled, keep the repair at the application policy source.
additions.sourceClaim: Prompt caching reuses matching prefix content; a changed tool or prompt block before the breakpoint creates a distinct prefix.
additions.auditFinding: Adds an integrated cache/observability diagnosis that attributes stale content to the application assembling P41, preserving exact provider-prefix semantics and separate freshness evidence.
additions.integrationConstraint: D3.4 requires policy-fetch revision, assembled-prefix revision, cache hit/miss, and outcome joins to diagnose stale application bytes; separate version and outcome joins must remain visible after the repair.

objectiveLabel: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat

existing.scenario: A procurement assistant has twenty available tools, but the current workflow only searches suppliers, retrieves one contract, and summarizes it; tool descriptions consume much of the initial context.
existing.evidence: Three read tools cover the current workflow; rare write and export tools remain needed by separately governed workflows.
existing.decisiveConstraint: Keep high-use precise schemas available and defer rare governed capabilities for on-demand discovery.
existing.expectedDecision: Load the three read tools for this path and defer the rare tools until their governed workflow is selected.
existing.rationale: Curation reduces context and selection pressure without deleting approved capabilities.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Expose every tool initially or remove all but a text generator.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: The first preserves the bloat, while the second turns a context problem into an unsupported manual process.
existing.counterfactual: If telemetry showed all twenty tools were required on nearly every request, eager loading could be justified after measuring the context cost.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends loading the most critical tools while deferring others for discovery when the tool inventory is large.
existing.auditFinding: The curation decision is sound, but option c is strictly longest; rewrite alternatives with comparable frequency, governance, and context detail.

existing.scenario: A finance assistant has four tools named fetch_invoice, search_invoice, lookup_invoice, and retrieve_invoice; they overlap but accept different filters, and the assistant often chooses a contract that cannot satisfy the request.
existing.evidence: The workflow needs identifier retrieval and bounded filtered search, each with a distinct valid input contract.
existing.decisiveConstraint: Each surviving tool should expose one distinct operation with predictable valid filters; overlapping names and contracts are causing selection errors.
existing.expectedDecision: Consolidate overlapping capability surfaces into canonical identifier and search tools with distinct descriptions and filters.
existing.rationale: Removing aliases clarifies the mapping from intent to one typed operation and makes selection failures testable.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Add more aliases, call all four tools on every request, or expose the database for arbitrary queries.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Those choices increase ambiguity, waste calls, or bypass typed and authorized boundaries.
existing.counterfactual: If each tool had a genuinely different backend capability and clear names, keeping multiple tools would be justified after separate selection tests.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic notes that tools with similar names can lead to wrong tool selection and incorrect parameters.
existing.auditFinding: The diagnosis is valid, but option b is strictly longest; rewrite alternatives with comparable overlap, contract, and authorization detail.

existing.scenario: A claims assistant receives every matching policy record, sometimes 10,000 rows, even when the user asks about one claim; the model then misses the relevant clause.
existing.evidence: The full result set must remain queryable, but the active context needs only bounded candidate fields and selected detail.
existing.decisiveConstraint: The active context needs bounded relevant results, while the full result set remains queryable through explicit continuation and detail paths.
existing.expectedDecision: Require bounded filters and pagination, return concise matches with a continuation token, and expose detail lookup by record ID.
existing.rationale: The service controls the result boundary so the assistant can request the next relevant slice without hiding records arbitrarily.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Return all rows and ask the model to summarize them, or truncate silently at ten rows.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: The first consumes attention before selection, while the second can hide the correct record and has no reliable continuation.
existing.counterfactual: If a backend aggregate answered the question without record evidence, expose the aggregate and a deliberate drill-down path rather than all raw rows.
existing.sourceClaim: Large intermediate tool results can pollute context; processing results before exposing only what is needed keeps the model focused.
existing.auditFinding: The result-boundary repair is valid, but option c is strictly longest; rewrite alternatives with comparable filtering, continuation, and evidence detail.

existing.scenario: A building-permit platform serves three municipalities through one MCP catalog of 80 tools; each municipality is authorized for a different subset, while three core reads dominate and regional forms and exports are rare.
existing.evidence: Core authorized tools should be immediate; discovery and invocation must enforce municipality and user scope.
existing.decisiveConstraint: Capability visibility and execution authorization must respect the requesting tenant and user while high-use authorized tools remain immediately available.
existing.expectedDecision: Keep each tenant's authorized core eager, defer its rare tools, scope discovery by validated tenant and user, and recheck authorization at invocation.
existing.rationale: This combines telemetry-guided curation with independent execution authorization at a multi-tenant boundary.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Load all 80 definitions for every tenant or delete every rare regional tool.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: The first exposes irrelevant or unauthorized capabilities and the second deletes valid long-tail behavior based only on frequency.
existing.counterfactual: If every municipality shared the same permissions and tool mix, one common curated inventory could replace tenant-specific filtering.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic describes loading frequent tools and deferring the rest, while the application still controls tool availability and execution.
existing.auditFinding: Controller inspected every canonical option: preserve the useful scenario and decision, but replace implausible distractors that advertise unsafe, unmeasured, untyped, arbitrary, or explicitly unverified behavior; provide professional competing actions that lose on the stated constraint and align per-option feedback.

additions.scenario: A single reporting tool exposes eighteen optional filters, four mutually exclusive output modes, and several nullable identifiers; malformed combinations cause frequent retries even though only ID lookup and date-bounded search are needed.
additions.evidence: Call logs show selection and schema errors cluster around invalid combinations, and the application can expose separate typed contracts for the two operations.
additions.decisiveConstraint: Each visible capability should have one narrow purpose and a parameter schema that makes invalid combinations unrepresentable or rejectable before execution.
additions.expectedDecision: Split the broad surface into an identifier lookup tool and a date-bounded search tool with required, typed fields; remove unused output modes from this workflow.
additions.rationale: The decision addresses schema and contract bloat inside one tool, which differs from duplicate tool names or oversized result payloads.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Keep one universal tool and add more prose telling the model which optional fields usually go together.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: More prose does not make invalid combinations impossible and leaves the model choosing among a large union schema.
additions.counterfactual: If all modes were exercised equally and a discriminated schema could validate them deterministically, one tool could remain after contract tests prove the boundary.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic warns that similar tool names and parameters can lead to wrong tools or incorrect parameters; applying that schema-clarity principle to a union-shaped tool is the scenario's design deduction.
additions.auditFinding: Uncovered decision: reduce capability bloat inside a union-shaped tool by splitting typed operations; this is distinct from duplicate names and result-size control.

additions.scenario: A security audit asks for counts by actor and day across 100,000 event records; the model needs the aggregate and a few event IDs for drill-down, not the raw rows.
additions.evidence: The service can filter and aggregate in code, return a compact summary with stable IDs, and fetch selected records separately when an analyst asks for evidence.
additions.decisiveConstraint: Large intermediate results must be processed before entering model context while preserving an explicit path to inspect source records.
additions.expectedDecision: Use programmatic or service-side filtering and aggregation, expose only the summary and representative IDs to the model, and provide a separate bounded detail call.
additions.rationale: This is a configuration decision about where intermediate computation occurs, beyond merely adding page limits to a search response.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Return all 100,000 events and ask Claude to calculate the grouping before writing the answer.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The raw result pollutes context, adds token and latency cost, and makes arithmetic depend on a model seeing every row.
additions.counterfactual: If the question required nuanced evidence from every event, retain a retrieval index and page selected records, but still avoid exposing the complete corpus by default.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends processing large intermediate tool results before exposing only the needed information to the model.
additions.auditFinding: Uncovered decision: process and aggregate large tool results before model exposure while retaining drill-down IDs; distinct from search pagination and tool-schema curation.

additions.scenario: A small internal assistant has five tools: search, fetch, update, notify, and close. All five are used by every request path, their typed definitions total 1% of context, and the server can enforce authorization at invocation.
additions.evidence: No rare capability remains to defer, and omitting any one tool causes a second discovery round that adds 400 ms; tool names and parameters are distinct.
additions.decisiveConstraint: The inventory is small, stable, and universally needed, so eager exposure is preferable to deferred discovery.
additions.expectedDecision: Load all five governed tool definitions in the initial request, retain server-side authorization and typed schemas, and reserve discovery for a future inventory change.
additions.rationale: The context and latency evidence reverses the large-inventory default: eager core plus deferred tail has no tail to defer here.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Use a discovery mechanism first and defer all tools because eager capability exposure is always harmful.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The definitions consume negligible context and every request needs them, so discovery adds avoidable latency and complexity.
additions.counterfactual: If the inventory grows or rare tools make up most definitions, restore a critical eager set and governed deferred discovery.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends loading the most critical tools while deferring others for discovery when the tool inventory is large.
additions.auditFinding: Flips the existing deferred-tail choice because all five tools are required and their definitions occupy only 1% of context.
additions.contrastBeforeDecision: The existing paired item has twenty tools, a small current subset, and descriptions that consume substantial initial context.
additions.contrastAfterDecision: This item has five tiny, universally used definitions, so deferred discovery adds latency without protecting context.

additions.scenario: After a catalog release adds twelve tools, wrong-tool selection rises from 0.5% to 4.2% while transport p95 stays unchanged. Two tools have similar names but different tenant filters, and traces record only the final answer, not the selected tool or inventory version.
additions.evidence: The application can publish canonical names and required typed fields, version the catalog, and record selected tool, parameters, authorization result, and outcome.
additions.decisiveConstraint: The capability surface needs schema clarity and observable selection outcomes; latency alone cannot identify or repair the new tool-choice failure.
additions.expectedDecision: Split overlapping capabilities into canonical tools with distinct required filters, version the inventory, and trace the selected tool, parameters, authorization, and result before expanding the catalog.
additions.rationale: The decision addresses both capability bloat and the evidence needed to determine whether the repair works.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Keep all tools visible and tune model temperature because the p95 transport metric is healthy.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The defect is wrong selection and parameters, not transport latency; extra visibility and randomness can increase the ambiguity.
additions.counterfactual: If traces show the errors come from a single malformed backend response rather than selection, repair that contract and keep the tool surface unchanged.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic notes that tools with similar names can lead to wrong tool selection and incorrect parameters.
additions.auditFinding: Adds a measured catalog-version and selection-trace diagnosis, distinct from the existing duplicate-name consolidation alone.
additions.integrationConstraint: D3.4 requires inventory-version, chosen-tool, parameter, authorization, and outcome spans to separate schema ambiguity from backend failure; if those traces show a backend defect, the expected repair changes.

objectiveLabel: Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps

existing.scenario: An enterprise MCP server exposes payroll over HTTP and forwards a user's bearer token to a downstream payroll service without checking audience or scopes.
existing.evidence: The token arrives over TLS, but the MCP resource server has not established that it was intended for this resource or permits the requested operation.
existing.decisiveConstraint: A bearer token must be intended for the current resource and carry the requested scope; a downstream resource needs its own least-privileged trust boundary.
existing.expectedDecision: Validate issuer, audience, expiry, and scopes at the resource server, then use a separately issued least-privileged downstream credential.
existing.rationale: Transport protection does not replace resource-specific authorization or a downstream trust boundary.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Trust the bearer token because TLS protects it, move it into a query parameter, or ask Claude to infer payroll permission.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Those choices preserve token confusion or move a security decision into model text.
existing.counterfactual: If the downstream service were the same resource server and explicitly accepted that audience and scope, token exchange would need a different design, but checks would remain.
existing.sourceClaim: The resource server must validate that the token is intended for it and must not forward a received token upstream to another resource server.
existing.auditFinding: The security diagnosis is correct, but option b is strictly longest; rewrite alternatives with comparable audience, scope, and trust-boundary detail.

existing.scenario: A web client starts an MCP authorization flow; the authorization server accepts any redirect URI under the company domain, and the client sends neither state nor PKCE.
existing.evidence: A broad redirect rule and missing response binding/code protection create separate authorization-code flow risks.
existing.decisiveConstraint: The authorization code flow must bind an exact destination and the response to its initiating session and client so redirection and interception cannot be treated as equivalent.
existing.expectedDecision: Require exact pre-registered redirect URIs, bind the response to the initiating session with state, and protect the code with PKCE.
existing.rationale: The repair addresses destination validation, response mix-up, and code interception at their respective protocol points.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Keep the broad redirect rule and place the authorization code in a fragment, or ask the user to paste it manually.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Neither alternative establishes exact destination or robust session and code binding.
existing.counterfactual: If the client were a confidential server-rendered app with a different code exchange profile, PKCE requirements could differ, but redirect and state validation would remain explicit.
existing.sourceClaim: MCP authorization requires exact redirect URI handling, state protection, and PKCE for the authorization-code flow.
existing.auditFinding: The protocol diagnosis is sound, but option b is strictly longest; rewrite alternatives with comparable redirect, state, and PKCE specificity.

existing.scenario: A developer runs a local MCP server as a child process over stdio on a locked workstation; a reviewer proposes applying HTTP bearer-token authorization to every message because the local database is sensitive.
existing.evidence: The transport is process-bound stdio, while HTTP authorization applies only when a resource is exposed over HTTP.
existing.decisiveConstraint: Credential protection must match the actual transport boundary: stdio relies on process and environment controls, while HTTP requires resource authorization.
existing.expectedDecision: Use process and environment controls for stdio credentials and apply MCP HTTP authorization requirements when the server is remotely exposed.
existing.rationale: Authentication controls must match the actual transport boundary rather than treating every message as HTTP.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Apply the HTTP authorization-server exchange to stdio messages, disable authentication because the process is local, or put passwords in tool descriptions.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: The first misapplies the protocol, the second assumes away local threats, and the third leaks secrets into model-visible metadata.
existing.counterfactual: If the child process were replaced by an HTTP listener reachable by other principals, the HTTP resource-server authorization requirements would become applicable.
existing.sourceClaim: MCP's HTTP authorization requirements differ from stdio, where environment and process controls protect credentials.
existing.auditFinding: The transport boundary is correct, but option c is strictly longest; rewrite alternatives with comparable process, environment, and HTTP detail.

existing.scenario: An expense assistant can call a billing API with model-supplied account_id and refund_amount; the backend trusts the fields, and a test reaches another tenant's account.
existing.evidence: The authenticated subject and tenant must be bound server-side to the requested resource and amount, with denial evidence.
existing.decisiveConstraint: The backend must bind requested tenant resources and refund side effects to the validated authenticated subject; model arguments cannot grant authority.
existing.expectedDecision: Derive identity from validated credentials, authorize account and refund scope at the backend, reject mismatches, and record denied attempts.
existing.rationale: This protects the side-effect boundary even when model arguments are manipulated or wrong.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Trust account_id because the prompt says to use the current account or let Claude redact suspicious requests.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Prompt wording and model judgment cannot enforce tenant binding or refund authorization.
existing.counterfactual: If the operation were read-only and returned no tenant data, the high-impact refund approval gate would not apply, but server-side resource authorization would still matter.
existing.sourceClaim: Access tokens should be restricted to the intended resource and scopes, with enforcement performed by the resource server.
existing.auditFinding: Controller inspected every canonical option: preserve the useful scenario and decision, but replace implausible distractors that advertise unsafe, unmeasured, untyped, arbitrary, or explicitly unverified behavior; provide professional competing actions that lose on the stated constraint and align per-option feedback.

additions.scenario: A payroll tool catalog exposes read, export, and adjustment operations; the user has payroll.read but not payroll.export or payroll.adjust, while the model can still see and request all three.
additions.evidence: Role and scope data are available before discovery, and the execution service can map each operation to a required scope and approval level.
additions.decisiveConstraint: Capability discovery and invocation must enforce operation-specific scopes; a logged-in identity alone is insufficient for export or mutation.
additions.expectedDecision: Expose only tools allowed by the current scope, require a server-side scope and approval check for export or adjustment, and reject requests that fail either check.
additions.rationale: This decision narrows the visible capability set and protects high-impact operations independently of prompt instructions.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Show all tools and tell Claude to choose read-only operations unless the user explicitly asks for more.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The model can be induced to call a visible operation, and an explicit user request does not grant the missing scope.
additions.counterfactual: If the user received a separately approved export scope, the export tool could be discovered and invoked under that scope while adjustment remained unavailable.
additions.sourceClaim: Access tokens should carry restricted scopes for the intended resource and the resource server enforces them; mapping those scopes to individual tool visibility and approval is the scenario's application design.
additions.auditFinding: Uncovered security decision: map individual tool capabilities to scopes and approval levels at discovery and execution; distinct from token audience validation and model-supplied resource IDs.

additions.scenario: A long-running agent discovers a payroll export tool while the user is authorized, but the user's role is revoked before the queued invocation reaches the server.
additions.evidence: The discovery result is cached, credentials can be refreshed or checked at invocation, and the server can record a rejected stale capability attempt.
additions.decisiveConstraint: Authorization must be re-evaluated at the execution boundary using current identity, token validity, and scope; discovery-time permission is not a durable grant.
additions.expectedDecision: Refresh or validate the current credential immediately before execution, reject the stale export handle if scope is gone, and audit the decision with the operation and subject.
additions.rationale: Rechecking closes revocation and time-of-check/time-of-use gaps in long-running agent plans.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Trust the cached discovery result because the user was authorized when the agent first saw the tool.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: A cached catalog can outlive role changes or token expiry and would turn a previously valid plan into an unauthorized action.
additions.counterfactual: If the capability were represented by a short-lived signed grant whose expiry and scope were verified atomically by the server, that grant check could replace a separate catalog refresh.
additions.sourceClaim: The resource server enforces the token's intended resource and scopes; requiring a current check at invocation after discovery is the scenario's revocation and time-of-check/time-of-use control.
additions.auditFinding: Uncovered security decision: recheck current authorization at invocation after capability discovery; distinct from initial catalog filtering and argument-level tenant binding.

additions.scenario: A local MCP server currently runs as a child process over stdio on a locked workstation. The same server is moved behind a shared HTTP endpoint for six remote clients, each with separate tenant scopes and user sessions.
additions.evidence: Process environment controls protected the local process, but the HTTP endpoint now receives bearer tokens and exposes resources across tenants; exact redirect, audience, scope, and invocation checks are available.
additions.decisiveConstraint: The transport boundary has changed, so local process controls no longer suffice; remote HTTP authorization and resource-server enforcement are required.
additions.expectedDecision: Use MCP HTTP authorization for the shared endpoint, validate issuer, audience, expiry, resource, and scopes at the resource server, and keep tenant binding and invocation checks independent of model arguments.
additions.rationale: The same logical tools require a different authorization strategy once they cross from local process isolation to a remote shared resource.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Keep stdio environment controls because the server code and tool names did not change.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: Remote clients are outside the protected process, so environment controls cannot bind a bearer token to its resource, tenant, or scope.
additions.counterfactual: If the server returns to a local child process with no remote exposure, use process and environment controls again, while keeping application authorization for sensitive operations.
additions.sourceClaim: MCP's HTTP authorization requirements differ from stdio, where environment and process controls protect credentials.
additions.auditFinding: Flips the existing local-stdio control decision when the same capability becomes a shared remote HTTP resource.
additions.contrastBeforeDecision: The existing paired item has a locked workstation and a child process connected only over stdio.
additions.contrastAfterDecision: This item moves the server behind a shared HTTP endpoint with remote tenant sessions.

additions.scenario: A user starts a large payroll export with a valid token. The export job is resumable, but the token expires during generation and the user role is revoked before the download artifact is released.
additions.evidence: The resource server can refresh or reauthorize the user, bind the export to the intended resource and scope, persist job state, and audit the requester and completion event. The download is a consequential side effect.
additions.decisiveConstraint: Authorization must be checked at each release boundary; a token valid at discovery cannot authorize a later artifact after expiry or revocation.
additions.expectedDecision: Persist the resumable job, stop release when the token or role is stale, reauthorize and recheck subject, resource, and scope before continuing, and publish only after the current authorization and audit record succeeds.
additions.rationale: The case integrates token lifecycle with durable workflow state so a safe pause is explicit and resumable.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Continue the job with the original token because its scope was valid when the tool was discovered, then log the expiry after delivery.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The token is expired and the role revoked before a consequential release; discovery-time authority cannot authorize a later artifact.
additions.counterfactual: If reauthorization succeeds with the same intended resource and scope, resume from the checkpoint; if it fails, retain the job as unavailable and do not expose the artifact.
additions.sourceClaim: The resource server must validate that the token is intended for it and must not forward a received token upstream to another resource server.
additions.auditFinding: Adds a token-expiry and revocation decision integrated with durable job state, beyond one-shot scope filtering.
additions.integrationConstraint: D1.2 requires a durable checkpoint and explicit outcome state for the resumable export; if current authorization is valid the job may continue, but if it is stale the expected decision changes to pause/reauthorize or unavailable.

objectiveLabel: Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions

existing.scenario: An insurance intake service must extract twelve fields within a 3-second p95 target; an efficient model reaches 2.1 seconds and 95% critical-field accuracy, while a stronger model reaches 4.8 seconds and 97%.
existing.evidence: The efficient candidate meets both stated pilot thresholds; the stronger candidate misses latency, and hard cases can be identified for follow-up evaluation.
existing.decisiveConstraint: The default must meet the service floor, while any quality escalation must be validated on end-to-end p95 and cost.
existing.expectedDecision: Use the efficient candidate as default after holdout validation and test confidence-based escalation to the stronger model for hard cases with end-to-end p95 and cost measurement.
existing.rationale: The configuration spends extra capability where it can improve quality without imposing a known SLA violation on every claim.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Use the stronger model for every claim, add an unmeasured validation call, or route all low-confidence cases without measuring the combined path.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Each alternative either violates the target or assumes a latency and cost result that has not been measured.
existing.counterfactual: If a stronger model later met the 3-second p95 target at the required volume, it could replace the default after the same quality and cost checks.
existing.sourceSection: When (and when not) to use agents
existing.sourceClaim: Agentic complexity trades latency and cost for performance, so the simplest configuration that meets the task needs should be measured first.
existing.auditFinding: The trade-off is valid, but option d is strictly longest; rewrite alternatives with comparable threshold, routing, and measurement detail.

existing.scenario: A contract analyst replaced a model after p95 fell from 4.2 seconds to 1.4 seconds, but indemnity misses rose from 3% to 11%; the team measured only averages.
existing.evidence: The decision-relevant clause slice regressed materially, and actual prompts, data, edge cases, and variants can be replayed.
existing.decisiveConstraint: A quality floor on the decision-relevant slice must be evaluated jointly with end-to-end latency and cost; average speed cannot justify a measured regression.
existing.expectedDecision: Compare quality, latency, and cost on the indemnity slice and other edge cases before choosing a route, prompt/context repair, or model upgrade.
existing.rationale: Average speed cannot justify a configuration that misses a required clause floor; slice evaluation reveals the real trade-off.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Keep the new model because p95 is the only measurable property, or add output tokens and assume omissions will recover.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: The first ignores task quality and the second changes output length without evidence that it restores clause recall.
existing.counterfactual: If held-out indemnity recall stayed within the agreed floor, the measured latency gain could justify retaining the faster model.
existing.sourceSection: When (and when not) to use agents
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends evaluating the actual task and adding complexity only when it improves the outcome enough to justify latency and cost.
existing.auditFinding: The diagnosis is valid, but option c is strictly longest; rewrite alternatives with comparable slice, latency, and cost detail.

existing.scenario: A claims workflow drafts a recommendation and then verifies its citations; sequential calls measure 2.4 seconds p95 and 96% citation correctness, while parallel calls measure 1.5 seconds and 88% because the verifier lacks the draft.
existing.evidence: The service requires p95 at or below 2.5 seconds and citation correctness at or above 95%; the verifier depends on the draft artifact.
existing.decisiveConstraint: The verifier depends on the draft artifact, so any parallel configuration must preserve that dependency and satisfy both latency and citation floors.
existing.expectedDecision: Keep the measured sequential dependency, pass the draft explicitly to verification, and continue validating joint p95 and correctness.
existing.rationale: Parallelism is not a win if it removes the evidence artifact needed to satisfy the accuracy floor.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Run both calls in parallel and add an unmeasured reconciliation call, or collapse them into one untested call.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Those changes hide the dependency and assume a latency or quality result that the pilot does not establish.
existing.counterfactual: If the verifier could consume a durable draft artifact produced before the request, independent calls could be parallelized after measuring the new path.
existing.sourceClaim: Sequential calls fit fixed subtasks when one step depends on the output of another; parallelization applies to independent subtasks.
existing.auditFinding: The dependency boundary is sound, but option b is strictly longest; rewrite alternatives with comparable artifact, threshold, and measurement detail.

existing.scenario: A research team produces nightly summaries of 500 long scientific reports; there is no interactive latency SLA, but synthesis quality, citations, and total spend are reviewed before distribution.
existing.evidence: A capability-first baseline can establish the quality and citation floor before lower-cost or staged routes are tested.
existing.decisiveConstraint: Batch model optimization must start from a measured synthesis and citation floor, then reduce cost only where the accepted outcome remains intact.
existing.expectedDecision: Measure quality, citations, and cost, then test a lower-cost model or staged route only where the accepted outcome floor holds.
existing.rationale: An overnight batch still needs evidence of outcome quality; absence of an interactive SLA changes the trade-off rather than removing it.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Choose the strongest model permanently or the cheapest model immediately without measuring synthesis quality.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: The first wastes spend without a capability test, and the second can distribute unsupported summaries.
existing.counterfactual: If a lower-cost route consistently met the citation and synthesis floor on representative reports, it could become the batch default.
existing.sourceClaim: For complex accuracy-sensitive work, Anthropic recommends starting capability-first, then evaluating and optimizing efficiency.
existing.auditFinding: Controller inspected every canonical option: preserve the useful scenario and decision, but replace implausible distractors that advertise unsafe, unmeasured, untyped, arbitrary, or explicitly unverified behavior; provide professional competing actions that lose on the stated constraint and align per-option feedback.

additions.scenario: A claims request fans out to four independent policy lookups; average latency is 1.6 seconds, but under production concurrency p95 reaches 3.8 seconds because the integration serializes the lookups before a dependent citation verifier.
additions.evidence: Load tests show the four lookups have no data dependency, while the verifier requires their combined evidence; the service target is 2.5 seconds p95 with a citation floor.
additions.decisiveConstraint: Only independent work may move off the critical path; the verifier must wait for all required evidence and the parallel route must be load-tested end to end.
additions.expectedDecision: Run the four independent lookups concurrently with bounded concurrency, aggregate their results, then invoke the verifier after the evidence barrier; measure p95, errors, and citation correctness under load.
additions.rationale: This targets integration critical-path latency and preserves the actual dependency rather than selecting a different model or trusting an average.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Parallelize the verifier before lookups finish and infer missing evidence, or optimize for the 1.6-second average without changing the serialized path.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The first breaks the evidence dependency and the second leaves the production tail above the SLA.
