additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic documents worktrees as separate working directories and branches for parallel sessions, and says a fresh worktree may require its own dependency and environment setup.
additions.auditFinding: New family: repair and verify fresh-worktree dependencies and environment before attributing a pre-test failure to the assistant, model, or patch.
additions.integrationConstraint: ccarp-7.3 requires a reproducible environment diagnosis; without setup evidence, the action changes from patch investigation to worktree provisioning.

additions.scenario: A narrowly scoped patch passes the independent contract fixtures, the diff contains only declared files, a fresh-context review finds no unmet criterion, and the owner has accepted the recorded evidence.
additions.evidence: The patch scope, independent test outputs, review criteria, reviewer context, and owner acceptance are all captured in the change record.
additions.decisiveConstraint: The defined acceptance evidence is complete and convergent; repeating another model review without a new risk or unmet criterion adds delay without improving the decision.
additions.expectedDecision: Accept the scoped patch, record the evidence and owner decision, and move to the agreed merge or rollout step; reopen review only if new evidence or scope changes appear.
additions.rationale: This adds an explicit stopping and acceptance decision after independent evidence is complete, complementing the existing requirement to obtain a fresh review when evidence is missing.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Keep requesting additional reviews and broader tests until every possible risk has been discussed, even though the declared criteria already pass.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: It replaces a defined acceptance boundary with open-ended review and cannot justify a new decision without a changed risk or requirement.
additions.counterfactual: If any declared criterion, independent fixture, or owner acceptance were missing, the existing adversarial-review boundary would still require blocking and review.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends a fresh-context review of the diff and explicit criteria before counting unattended work as done.
additions.auditFinding: New boundary-to-transfer family: when declared scope, independent checks, fresh review, and owner acceptance all converge, accept and stop rather than add review without a new risk.
additions.integrationConstraint: ccarp-6.5 requires an owned phase decision and explicit acceptance evidence; when all declared evidence converges, the action changes from review to acceptance and lifecycle progression.

objectiveLabel: Support debugging and operational issue resolution

existing.scenario: A developer reports that a project MCP server is missing, a hook does not fire, and behavior differs between two repository directories.
existing.evidence: The developer can inspect loaded status, approvals, project-root files, relative command paths, and targeted MCP debug output without resetting the setup.
existing.decisiveConstraint: The directory difference and loaded configuration are diagnostic evidence; a reset or model change would erase or bypass the likely cause.
existing.expectedDecision: Inspect setup and loaded status, check /mcp approval and connection state, compare project paths and relative commands, then enable targeted debug logging.
existing.rationale: The debugging sequence is sound, but the accepted option is longest and most detailed; rewrite alternatives with comparable status, scope, path, and log checks.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Reinstall the tools, change the model, or copy everything into user scope before inspecting the failing directory.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Those discard configuration evidence or change unrelated layers without explaining project approval, path, or hook loading behavior.
existing.counterfactual: If status and paths were identical in both directories and the server failed only at the provider, local reinstall would not address the remaining remote failure.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends /mcp for connection and approval status, targeted MCP debug logging, and checking project paths and relative commands when servers fail.
existing.auditFinding: Underlying debugging sequence is valid, but the accepted option is longest and most complete; rewrite choices with parallel read-only status and path hypotheses.

existing.scenario: Claude Code uses high CPU in a large repository, while a fresh session with customizations disabled is normal and the current conversation contains large build outputs.
existing.evidence: The operator can checkpoint a safe summary, compare compacted or restarted sessions, run safe mode, and re-enable one customization at a time; diagnostics may contain sensitive content.
existing.decisiveConstraint: The controlled difference implicates context or a customization, so isolation must preserve evidence and avoid exposing heap or conversation contents.
existing.expectedDecision: Compact or restart, reproduce in safe mode, re-enable plugins, MCP servers, or hooks one at a time, and treat detailed diagnostics as sensitive.
existing.rationale: The controlled diagnosis is correct, but the accepted option is longest; rewrite alternatives with comparable context, customization, and data-handling tests.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Add more build output, share a heap snapshot publicly, or change model size before isolating local customizations.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: More output worsens load, heap data can contain credentials, and model size does not identify a local context or customization cause.
existing.counterfactual: If safe mode and a fresh compact session both reproduced the same CPU spike with no customization, investigate the repository, runtime, or provider path instead.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends compacting, restarting, and using safe mode to isolate customizations, and warns that heap snapshots can contain conversations and credentials.
existing.auditFinding: Underlying isolation diagnosis is valid, but the accepted option is materially longer and more specific; rewrite alternatives with equally concrete reproduction and data-handling actions.

existing.scenario: An operations team is writing a support runbook that must correlate API failures without logging sensitive prompts and isolate a suspected MCP plugin without changing organization policy.
existing.evidence: Request IDs and classified errors can link redacted events, while safe mode provides a reversible comparison for a plugin or hook.
existing.decisiveConstraint: The runbook must preserve correlation and isolation evidence within the sensitive-data and managed-policy boundaries.
existing.expectedDecision: Use request-level identifiers and redacted default telemetry for correlation, then isolate the customization in safe mode without weakening managed policy.
existing.rationale: The accepted controls are independent, reversible, and fit the stated privacy and policy boundaries; the distractors create exposure or amplify failures.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Log full prompts and credentials, retry without a bound, or remove managed policy to make diagnosis easier.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Those expose sensitive data, amplify outages, or expand authority when targeted correlation and safe-mode isolation are available.
existing.counterfactual: If the incident were a local non-sensitive prototype with no managed policy or remote credentials, verbose temporary logs could be acceptable during a controlled reproduction.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends safe mode to test plugins, MCP servers, and hooks, and warns that detailed diagnostics may contain conversation content or credentials.
existing.auditFinding: Preserve request-level correlation, redacted diagnostics, and reversible safe-mode isolation; replace full-prompt logging, unbounded retries, and policy removal with one credible diagnostic path that loses privacy, recovery, or policy scope, and align feedback.

existing.scenario: A CI job runs Claude Code noninteractively and intermittently fails: some responses are transient overloads, while others are malformed requests caused by configuration. It currently retries every failure and emits only an exit code.
existing.evidence: The job can emit structured status, error type, request ID, and attempt count and can assign invalid configuration to the owning repository.
existing.decisiveConstraint: Recovery depends on provider error classification; bounded retry is appropriate only for eligible transient failures, while malformed requests need visible correction.
existing.expectedDecision: Emit structured evidence, preserve request IDs, back off only on documented transient errors, and fail visibly with an owner for malformed configuration.
existing.rationale: The recovery policy is correct, but the accepted option is longest and most detailed; rewrite alternatives with comparable classification, retry, and ownership scope.
existing.plausibleAlternative: Retry every failure indefinitely or change the prompt while hiding the response body.
existing.whyAlternativeLoses: Retries amplify invalid requests and hiding error evidence prevents diagnosis; prompt wording cannot repair malformed configuration.
existing.counterfactual: If every response were a documented transient overload with retry-after and configuration were validated before launch, bounded backoff could be the only runtime recovery branch.
existing.sourceClaim: Anthropic documents distinct error types, retry-after semantics, exponential backoff for transient failures, and a separate spend-cap condition that keeps failing until access resumes.
existing.auditFinding: Underlying recovery transfer is valid, but the accepted option is materially longer and more specific; rewrite alternatives with parallel error classification and recovery policies.

additions.scenario: After a plugin update, claude -p fails in CI while an interactive local session succeeds on the same repository and prompt. A known-good plugin version and safe mode are available.
additions.evidence: CI environment details, resolved settings, plugin versions, request IDs, and safe-mode results can be captured before changing the prompt or model. CI parity, pinned inputs, and rollback are scenario-provided incident controls.
additions.decisiveConstraint: The incident must be reproduced in the failing execution mode and customization state before a broad reinstall or model change; rollback must remain reversible.
additions.expectedDecision: Capture resolved configuration and versions, reproduce the noninteractive CI path with pinned inputs, compare safe mode, bisect or roll back the plugin, and preserve correlation evidence.
additions.rationale: Uncovered decision: isolate execution-environment and plugin drift through parity reproduction and reversible rollback; current rows cover MCP status, local safe mode, and provider error classes but not CI-only customization drift. The cited claim supports safe-mode customization isolation; CI parity and rollback are scenario-authored.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Change the prompt or model, reinstall every integration, or treat the local interactive success as proof CI is misreporting.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: Those change multiple variables and erase the execution-mode evidence needed to identify the plugin or resolved-setting difference.
additions.counterfactual: If the same pinned run failed in safe mode locally and in CI with identical resolved settings, the customization hypothesis would lose and provider, authentication, or request-shape evidence should lead.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends safe mode to test plugins, MCP servers, and hooks, and warns that detailed diagnostics may contain conversation content or credentials.
additions.auditFinding: Uncovered decision: reproduce CI-only failures in the same execution mode, isolate customization drift with safe mode, and use reversible rollback; current rows do not test environment parity.

additions.scenario: A CI job fails before receiving any HTTP response. DNS resolution and TLS/proxy diagnostics are captured, while no provider request identifier or response error body exists.
additions.evidence: The transport-layer evidence, destination configuration, and execution environment can be compared; the API error documentation distinguishes response errors and request identifiers.
additions.decisiveConstraint: Without an HTTP response there is no provider response identifier to correlate, so the first diagnosis must follow the client, DNS, proxy, or TLS path rather than escalate a provider request-ID incident.
additions.expectedDecision: Preserve the transport evidence, verify DNS/proxy/TLS and environment configuration, reproduce from the failing runner, and only use provider request-ID analysis after a request reaches the provider and returns a response.
additions.rationale: This is a true pre-response reversal of the existing request-ID and error-classification paths: the absence of a response changes the diagnostic layer.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Open a provider incident with a synthetic request ID or keep retrying the same job until a request identifier appears.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: A locally invented identifier cannot correlate a provider execution, and retries do not explain a deterministic transport failure without new evidence.
additions.counterfactual: If an HTTP response and request ID were present, preserve that ID and classify the documented error before choosing retry or owner routing as in the existing transfer item.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic includes a unique request ID in responses and errors so operators can correlate a failing request with their own traces and support investigations.
additions.auditFinding: New reversal family: when DNS, proxy, or TLS fails before an HTTP response, diagnose the runner transport path and do not fabricate provider correlation evidence.
additions.integrationConstraint: ccarp-4.6 requires transport and request telemetry joined at the application boundary; before an HTTP response, the action changes from provider correlation to runner/network diagnosis.

additions.scenario: A failure remains in safe mode, but a clean user and project configuration makes the same bounded task succeed. Authentication, model, built-in tools, permissions, managed hooks, and managed settings remain unchanged during the comparison.
additions.evidence: The clean-configuration result, safe-mode result, resolved user/project files, and managed policy/environment state can be compared without disabling organization controls.
additions.decisiveConstraint: Safe mode removes customizations but leaves core execution and managed controls active; success only under clean user/project configuration points to those configuration layers, not automatically to an external provider.
additions.expectedDecision: Compare and remove or correct the implicated user/project setting, keep managed policy intact, rerun the bounded reproduction, and escalate externally only if the clean configuration and managed/environment checks also fail.
additions.rationale: This adds the documented clean-configuration branch and corrects the overbroad inference that persistent safe-mode failure proves an external cause.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Bisect plugins further or bypass managed settings and change the provider/model because safe mode still failed.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The clean-configuration contrast already isolates user/project settings, while plugin bisection and policy bypass change the wrong layer and can violate team controls.
additions.counterfactual: If both safe mode and a clean user/project configuration failed after managed policy and environment checks matched, then a repository, runtime, or external-service investigation would be justified.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic notes that safe mode disables customizations while authentication, model, built-in tools, permissions, and managed hooks/settings remain; comparing a clean configuration isolates user and project settings.
additions.auditFinding: New reversal family: a safe-mode failure with clean user/project success isolates configuration layers; do not infer an external cause or bypass managed controls.
additions.integrationConstraint: ccarp-7.1 requires managed settings to remain enforced during diagnosis; if clean user/project configuration succeeds, the action changes to scope repair rather than policy bypass.

additions.scenario: Metadata and redacted timing are insufficient to reproduce a high-memory incident. The organization has explicitly authorized a private diagnostic sample with a named operator, restricted storage, and deletion date; support does not need routine prompt retention.
additions.evidence: The authorization, access list, retention date, bounded reproduction, and sensitive diagnostic handling procedure are recorded before capture.
additions.decisiveConstraint: Sensitive diagnostics should remain absent from routine telemetry, but an explicitly authorized, bounded capture is justified when lower-sensitivity evidence cannot answer the incident.
additions.expectedDecision: Capture only the approved diagnostic sample in restricted storage, record access and deletion, use it for the bounded reproduction, then remove it under the agreed retention rule; keep routine logs redacted.
additions.rationale: This is a controlled exception to the existing redacted-default boundary, with authorization and purpose limitation as the reversal conditions.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Either log full prompts and heap data in the normal incident stream or refuse every diagnostic capture even after the authorized metadata-only investigation is exhausted.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: Routine full capture creates unnecessary exposure, while blanket refusal prevents a proportionate incident investigation that the organization has explicitly authorized and bounded.
additions.counterfactual: If no named authorization, restricted storage, or deletion rule existed, remain with redacted metadata and safe-mode reproduction rather than collecting detailed diagnostics.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends safe mode first and explains that detailed diagnostics or heap snapshots can contain conversation content and credentials, so sensitive captures require careful handling.
additions.auditFinding: New reversal family: permit a narrowly authorized private diagnostic capture only after metadata and redacted reproduction are insufficient, with access and deletion controls.
additions.integrationConstraint: ccarp-5.4 requires an approved data-handling and retention boundary for sensitive diagnostic material; without it, remain redacted and do not capture detailed evidence.

additions.scenario: The provider returns a response that passes the requested structured-output schema, but the CI consumer rejects it because the consumer still expects an older field version. Request latency and provider availability are normal.
additions.evidence: The raw response, invocation schema, consumer schema version, and CI parser error are available; the provider response and transport status are valid.
additions.decisiveConstraint: A valid provider response does not prove compatibility with the downstream consumer; the failure is at the invocation/consumer contract boundary, not provider availability.
additions.expectedDecision: Compare and version the producer and consumer schemas, update or roll back the consumer contract through its change process, add a contract test for the accepted structured output, and rerun CI before changing provider retries.
additions.rationale: This adds a downstream structured-output contract diagnosis, which the existing provider error and request-ID items do not cover.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Retry the provider, switch models, or increase timeout because the CI job reports a response failure.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The response is valid and timely; provider changes cannot repair a consumer that rejects a known schema version.
additions.counterfactual: If the provider returned an invalid body or an HTTP error before the consumer saw a response, provider error classification and request correlation would become the relevant branch.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic recommends claude -p for CI and scripts, structured output for programmatic processing, and restricted tools when running unattended.
additions.auditFinding: New family: when a valid structured response is rejected downstream, repair the versioned producer-consumer contract and test it before investigating provider availability.
additions.integrationConstraint: ccarp-6.4 requires a versioned producer/consumer interface and acceptance check; if the consumer rejects a valid response, repair that contract rather than alter provider availability assumptions.

additions.scenario: A bounded reproduction still shows high memory after safe mode and a clean session. Diagnostics indicate native allocations dominate while the JavaScript heap remains within its normal range; the team proposes taking a JavaScript heap snapshot first.
additions.evidence: The troubleshooting diagnostics classify native versus JavaScript memory, and the operator can collect lower-sensitivity runtime and repository evidence before any private snapshot.
additions.decisiveConstraint: A JavaScript heap snapshot is useful for a JavaScript-heap problem; native-memory dominance requires a native/runtime or repository-load investigation and does not become actionable by inspecting an ordinary JS heap.
additions.expectedDecision: Preserve the classification, investigate the native-memory path and bounded repository/runtime reproduction, and reserve a private JavaScript heap snapshot for a case where JavaScript heap growth is the measured issue.
additions.rationale: This adds a resource-diagnosis reversal based on the documented memory classification rather than repeating safe-mode or customization isolation.
additions.plausibleAlternative: Take a full JavaScript heap snapshot immediately because it is the most detailed artifact available, or switch models to reduce memory.
additions.whyAlternativeLoses: The measured memory class makes a JS snapshot low-yield, and model changes do not identify native allocations or repository/runtime causes.
additions.counterfactual: If JavaScript heap usage dominated and remained high after safe-mode and clean-session checks, a private heap snapshot could be the appropriate next diagnostic under the documented sensitive-data handling.
additions.sourceClaim: Anthropic's troubleshooting guidance says to try safe mode first, distinguish JavaScript-heap from native-memory pressure, and handle any heap snapshot as sensitive diagnostic data.
additions.auditFinding: New reversal family: native-memory evidence changes the next diagnostic from JavaScript heap inspection to runtime or repository investigation; a detailed artifact is not automatically the right artifact.
additions.integrationConstraint: ccarp-4.6 requires resource evidence and a monitored owner for the incident; native-memory evidence changes the diagnostic path, while missing classification keeps deeper capture deferred.
